frameworks.name: Passion Attacking the Market
frameworks.definition: A competitive strategy where founders apply genuine personal passion to a market niche, enabling them to out-compete data-driven corporate competitors who lack that passion; the passion provides resilience and differentiation that purely analytic market-followers cannot replicate.

frameworks.name: Small Battles Compounding Framework
frameworks.definition: A progressive confidence-building method where a founder takes on one small winnable battle, then compounds those wins weekly until the battles themselves snowball in scale relative to the founder's growing capability; the mechanism is repeated small wins building identity and capability.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, CEO, ~2026) asserts that sustained performance across a competitive field depends less on motivation on any given day and more on the unconditional commitment to show up regardless of internal state, because the days with zero motivation are statistically as likely to produce pivotal creative breakthroughs as high-motivation days. According to LaVecchia, many of his most productive days at Bloom came specifically on days when he woke up with no motivation and showed up anyway.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to founders with an autonomous schedule who could skip work without external accountability
Applies to creative or entrepreneurial work where output is non-linear
claims.mechanism: Showing up increases the probability of a creative breakthrough on any given day; since creative ideas cannot be forced, volume of presence is the only reliable input that raises the likelihood of producing them.
bounded_by: LaVecchia does not claim the breakthrough always comes on low-motivation days, only that it is no less likely

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) observed that people watching him perform on his lowest physical days — when he had severe allergic reactions — could not detect any difference in his output quality. LaVecchia uses this as evidence that the performer's internal state is nearly invisible to the audience, and therefore the cost of going through the motions is almost always lower than the perceived cost of delaying.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to professional interactions such as pitches, calls, and meetings
Applies when the founder has the physical ability to show up, even if feeling poor
claims.mechanism: External observers lack visibility into internal state; what feels catastrophic internally registers as normal externally, making delay or avoidance a net-negative decision.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) contends that some people stop pursuing entrepreneurship not because of external failure but because it came too easily to them — natural ability removed the necessity of sustained effort, so they never built the habit of working hard. LaVecchia cites this as a reason people with clear entrepreneurial talent and the right behaviors still quit.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to individuals with high natural ability in a domain
claims.mechanism: When success comes easily, the individual never develops the behavioral habit of sustained effort; at the first real difficulty, they lack the trained tolerance to continue.
bounded_by: LaVecchia also cites that some people stop simply because they were never cut out to be entrepreneurs — ease of prior success is not the only cause

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) argues that the primary competitive strategy in the nutrition and beverage space is outlasting competitors who get comfortable after early revenue success. LaVecchia attributes Bloom's competitive position in part to competitors making early money, getting comfortable, and exiting the race — not to Bloom being categorically superior in product or marketing.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to competitive CPG categories (nutrition, beverage) with moderate barriers to entry and high early-stage dropouts
claims.mechanism: Competitors enter, achieve early revenue, become comfortable, and voluntarily reduce competitive effort; founders who maintain competitive intensity inherit market share by default.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) asserts that self-belief is not a prerequisite for entrepreneurial action but an output of it. A founder with no track record or a negative track record should begin with one small winnable battle per month, then accelerate to one per week, then one per day. The battles themselves scale in absolute difficulty relative to the founder's capability, but after roughly six months of this compounding, the founder's identity has transformed — the person they were before is no longer recognizable.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to founders at zero or negative track record
Applies across the first 6-12 months of entrepreneurial action
claims.mechanism: Small wins compound into identity change; each completed battle provides evidence of capability that the brain integrates, shifting self-concept from outsider to entrepreneur without requiring prior success as input.

anchors.value: one small battle per day, each larger in absolute terms than starting-phase battles

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) asserts that the physiological and psychological foundations of peak entrepreneurial performance are simple and well-known: consistent quality sleep of 7+ hours per night in a cold, dark room at the same time each day; high-protein whole-food eating; and daily physical activity of any modality. LaVecchia argues that executing these three consistently for two to three months produces a level of cognitive and physical performance that makes it extremely difficult for contemporaries who are not doing the same to compete.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to founders in their 20s and 30s
Requires minimum two to three months of consistent adherence before compounding effects are detectable
claims.mechanism: Physical health variables (sleep quality, nutrition, exercise) directly modulate cognitive output; consistent adherence over months produces compounding effects that intermittent adherence cannot replicate.

numbers.axis: minimum sleep duration for sustained high performance

anchors.value: up to 1 hour variation in bedtime/wake time

bounded_by: LaVecchia acknowledges some individuals have autoimmune or dietary constraints that limit the applicability of standard diet advice; he applies his own version accordingly

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) argues that chasing money as the primary goal is structurally inferior to chasing greatness or building something large, because wealth is a byproduct of the latter but not reliably achievable by optimizing for the former. LaVecchia supports this with his own experience: he never set financial targets but arrived at significant wealth by targeting product quality and distribution scale.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to consumer product and brand-building contexts
Applies to founders with sufficiently long time horizons (LaVecchia's timeline was approximately 10-12 years)
claims.mechanism: Building genuinely excellent products at scale creates customer value that monetizes; optimizing for money without that value creation loop produces neither lasting wealth nor satisfaction.
bounded_by: LaVecchia does not argue against making money; he argues against treating it as the primary optimization target

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) asserts that founders who sell their businesses — even for over $100 million — frequently become severely depressed, not because of the money itself but because they leave the life of pursuit. LaVecchia reports knowing multiple individuals who sold businesses for over $100 million and describe them as having some of the worst mental health he has encountered. His diagnosis: the money does not cause depression; exiting the pursuit does.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to founders who built identity around building; may not apply to founders with strong off-business purpose and identity
claims.mechanism: Founders who build around a pursuit-based identity lose their primary source of meaning at the moment of exit; the financial gain fails to replace the psychological function the pursuit served.

numbers.axis: sale price at which depression onset was observed

anchors.value: sale price is not the variable; loss of pursuit is

bounded_by: LaVecchia explicitly states money itself does not cause depression; the mechanism is exiting pursuit, not receiving wealth

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) reports a specific personal observation: posting content about a private trip on social media immediately shifted his emotional state from contentment to competitiveness, jealousy, and combativeness. For the first two days of the trip when he did not post, he felt entirely present and emotionally satisfied. After posting and receiving views and comments, he woke the next day feeling negative emotions he had not felt in months. This led him to conclude that external validation consistently produces the opposite of intrinsic fulfillment.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies when external validation is tied to public display of success markers (yacht, travel, wealth)
Condition: the person has existing chip-on-shoulder competitive drivers
claims.mechanism: Public sharing activates competitive and comparative cognition; once activated, the brain shifts from contentment-seeking to status-defense mode, producing anxiety, jealousy, and combativeness that displace intrinsic satisfaction.
bounded_by: LaVecchia notes this is his personal experience; he does not claim universal applicability across all personality types

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) contends that fear and paranoia are necessary fuel in early-stage entrepreneurship but become unnecessary and eventually counterproductive once the founder achieves financial freedom and business stability. In the early stage, the only mechanism to grow entrepreneurial skill is to convert fear into courage and win battles. Once the battles are won and financial freedom is achieved, the same skill operates without fear as fuel — it becomes internalized craft.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Early stage: fear is productive and necessary
Later stage (financial freedom achieved, business stable): fear is no longer the primary driver and its absence does not hurt performance
claims.mechanism: Fear converts into action when the alternative (failure, destitution) is live; once financial freedom is reached, the survival signal disappears but the behavioral pattern has been internalized as skill, enabling continued performance without the fear stimulus.
bounded_by: LaVecchia specifies this applies to him specifically at Bloom's current stage; he does not universalize that all fear disappears for all founders at financial freedom

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) asserts that passion applied to a market creates a durable competitive advantage over corporate competitors who follow only data and market signals, because the passion-driven competitor continues when data would indicate retreat, finds white space that analytics miss, and sustains intensity longer than incentive-driven suits can. LaVecchia attributes Bloom's success in the women's health and wellness segment specifically to competing with passion against publicly traded companies following data.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies when founder's passion intersects meaningfully with an underserved or mispriced market segment
Applies in CPG and consumer brand categories where authenticity and founder identity are perceivable by customers
claims.mechanism: Passion provides resilience through the down periods that purely data-driven operators abandon; corporate competitors optimize for efficiency and follow data signals, while passion-driven founders explore white space by following conviction, enabling breakthrough rather than incremental improvement.
bounded_by: LaVecchia advises that the passion must connect to a real white-space opportunity in a larger market; passion alone without a market angle does not confer advantage

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) argues that wealth is fundamentally a patience problem rather than an income problem. He illustrates this with his own timeline: Bloom's current scale (Bloom in over 70,000 doors worldwide, on track for over half a billion in revenue as of 2026) took approximately 10-12 years to build. Attempting to shortcut this by optimizing for near-term income rather than building something of genuine value would have resulted in a smaller outcome.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to consumer product companies building brand-driven distribution over time
LaVecchia's specific context: CPG, nutrition and beverage, mass retail distribution

numbers.axis: time required to build significant wealth via brand building

anchors.value: 70,000+ doors worldwide, over $500M revenue annually on track

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) asserts that critics and doubters are almost always people performing worse than the target of their criticism, never those performing better. LaVecchia states he has never personally received negative commentary or bad vibes from anyone he perceives as outperforming him, while negative commentary consistently originates from people he considers below him in the hierarchy of results. He interprets mockery of his personal brand initiative as jealousy from people who are not taking comparable moonshots.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
claims.speaker_term: nobody above you speaks down to you
conditions: Applies to criticism of public entrepreneurial initiatives (personal brand building, company building)
LaVecchia's experience is within his social and professional peer network
bounded_by: LaVecchia acknowledges this is his personal observation, not a universal study

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) argues that the most effective response to an environment of doubters and negative social pressure in early-stage entrepreneurship is geographic relocation to remove the source of friction, rather than attempting to change others' opinions. He and his wife Mari drove from their home to Boulder, Colorado — a city they had never visited — with all their possessions in a single vehicle, specifically to remove social friction and enable 18 months of uninterrupted focused work, during which Bloom Nutrition was launched.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies specifically in early-stage entrepreneurship when social environment produces resistance
Condition: founder has enough flexibility to physically relocate; does not apply to founders with location-dependent businesses or dependents requiring stability
claims.mechanism: Removing the source of social friction eliminates the emotional processing cost of managing criticism; isolation focuses cognitive and emotional resources on output rather than defense.

numbers.axis: duration of focused isolation at launch

anchors.region: LaVecchia and Mari's Bloom launch period in Boulder, Colorado
anchors.value: 18 months, no social relationships formed outside each other and their dog

bounded_by: LaVecchia frames this as a useful option for early-stage founders, not a requirement for all; he notes that he now manages criticism differently from how 21-year-old Greg did

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) asserts that the most valuable thing a successful founder can pass to a child is accumulated wisdom and skills, not financial wealth. LaVecchia argues that experiential wisdom that allows the child to skip the founding generation's painful learning curve provides a far greater competitive advantage than any financial inheritance, enabling the child to attempt greater challenges than the parent ever could.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to founders with young children who have both wealth and accumulated operational knowledge to transfer
claims.mechanism: Financial capital depreciates in value relative to the market's baseline; experiential wisdom accelerates capability development by eliminating error-driven learning costs, compounding the child's starting position above the parent's starting position.
bounded_by: LaVecchia acknowledges uncertainty about where the world is heading and explicitly refrains from claiming wisdom transfer is universally superior; he frames it as his personal conviction

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) argues that entrepreneurs must choose and commit to a single playbook rather than attempting to run multiple frameworks simultaneously. LaVecchia explicitly advises against running a hundred playbooks at once, framing single-playbook commitment as the prerequisite to becoming a great entrepreneur.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to early-stage and growth-stage entrepreneurs consuming multiple business education frameworks simultaneously

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) argues that the most successful people he knows personally have a committed significant other, and that a supportive partner is a critical accelerant to becoming the founder or professional you are trying to become. LaVecchia frames his wife Mari as not merely a supporter but as directly responsible for the trajectory of Bloom and for shaping his own character as a founder.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to male founders in consumer product and brand-building contexts based on LaVecchia's immediate peer set
LaVecchia acknowledges this is based on personal observation of people he knows
bounded_by: LaVecchia qualifies that the support type needed varies person to person; the critical variable is a partner who supports you in the way you specifically need

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) asserts that founding and maintaining a personal brand and publishing content is the only reliable way a founder controls their own reputation narrative. As Bloom grew large and LaVecchia remained unknown, he recognized that a reputation would form from public assumptions in a vacuum. The mechanism is that a creator who publishes controls the informational inputs; a founder who does not publish cedes narrative control to others' interpretations of the company's signals.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies when a company brand is becoming significantly larger than the founder's personal profile
Condition: the founder operates in a consumer-facing industry where public perception of leadership matters
claims.mechanism: In the absence of founder-generated narrative, audiences construct assumptions based on available signals (product, company culture rumors, financials); content creation fills that signal vacuum with accurate, intentional framing.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, ~2026) contends that comparison to other entrepreneurs is healthy when it produces inspiration but becomes destructive when it produces jealousy that drives emotional decisions aimed at beating a specific competitor rather than building something globally great. LaVecchia's operational rule: when he notices jealousy driving decisions toward beating a specific individual, he immediately unfollows or mutes that person.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Applies to founder psychology in competitive markets with visible peer comparisons on social media
The tipping point is when emotional decisions are being made to beat a specific person rather than to build something great
claims.mechanism: Jealousy-driven comparison shifts cognitive focus from long-horizon value creation to short-horizon status competition, degrading decision quality by anchoring it to a narrow adversarial frame rather than the founder's actual north star.
bounded_by: LaVecchia affirms competition and comparison are healthy when the signal is inspiration; only jealousy triggers the removal action

examples.text: Greg LaVecchia describes waking up at least one day per week with a severe autoimmune allergic reaction that causes cognitive fog, physical swelling, and difficulty getting out of bed. On these days he has to physically drag his legs out of bed. Despite this, he shows up to work regardless. He uses these days as evidence that the external output quality is indistinguishable from his best days — observers have no ability to detect he is suffering.

Greg LaVecchia describes the founding of Bloom Nutrition as a case study in geographic isolation enabling entrepreneurial output. He and his wife Mari, with no prior knowledge of the city, drove a blue Toyota 4Runner from their home to Boulder, Colorado, with all their possessions and their dog. They spent 18 months in Boulder without forming a single friendship outside each other, working exclusively, and launched Bloom Nutrition's first three products — an all-natural pre-workout in pina colada, green apple, and grapefruit flavors — during this period.

Greg LaVecchia describes being on a yacht with family and close friends in Europe for a three-week vacation. For the first two days he did not post to social media and felt entirely present, joyful, and emotionally stable — jet skiing, swimming, and engaging with family without competitive thoughts. On the third day he posted a photo; it received 200,000-300,000 views and mixed comments. The next morning he woke up feeling jealous, combative, and competitive — including feeling animosity toward people he had already surpassed, re-experiencing the feeling of chips being broken off his shoulders. He describes this reversal as stark and directly attributable to the social media post.

Greg LaVecchia describes knowing multiple people who sold their businesses for over $100 million and subsequently became severely depressed. He observes that society misattributes this depression to the financial outcome (having $100M) when the actual cause is exiting the pursuit itself. He reports firsthand that these are among the people with the worst mental health he has personally encountered.

Greg LaVecchia describes launching a personal brand Instagram and YouTube presence at age 31, shortly after becoming a father and while running Bloom at significant scale. People within his extended social circle — not his inner circle but acquaintances — mocked him to his face, calling him an influencer in a derogatory way. He reframes their mockery as confirmation that he was taking a moonshot they were not willing to take, and later used the initiative to control the narrative around his identity as Bloom grew.

Greg LaVecchia explains that Bloom began as a men's health and wellness brand focused on fitness supplements, reflecting his personal passion. He and Mari identified that all existing products were heavily masculine, leaving a white space in female health and wellness. By pursuing that white space — not purely because it was a market opportunity but because LaVecchia discovered he was passionate about making health products accessible to everyone — Bloom became the market leader in its category while competing against publicly traded companies and corporate boardrooms following only data.

practices.text: Show up every day regardless of motivation level. If creative or inspired work does not come, go through the motions — the physical act of showing up maintains the habit and increases the probability of a breakthrough on any given day.
On high-stakes calls or meetings where you feel terrible, do it anyway. You will almost certainly outperform your internal prediction and the other party will be unable to detect your low state.

Prioritize getting 7+ hours of quality sleep in a cold, dark room at the same consistent bedtime and wake time with no more than one hour of variation. Treat this as the foundation before adding any other health optimization.
Exercise every single day through any modality — walks, weight training, rowing — and prioritize outdoor activity in sunlight when possible.
After a period of celebration, rest, or vacation, get back on schedule as fast as possible. A step back should be followed by two forward; never extend recovery beyond what genuinely refreshes.

When you notice jealousy of a specific person is driving your business decisions rather than pursuit of building something great, immediately unfollow or mute that person to remove the emotional stimulus.

If you are in an early-stage entrepreneurial environment surrounded by people who mock or doubt your efforts and you cannot manage the emotional cost of that criticism, relocate physically away from it. There is no shame in running from the fight in the beginning; return later with results.

Build a personal brand and publish content to control your own narrative. If you do not create your own public-facing identity, the world will construct one from assumptions in the information vacuum.
Focus on one playbook and commit to it fully rather than trying to run multiple entrepreneurial frameworks simultaneously.
Keep people in your close circle who knew you before success and who will keep you grounded; intentionally maintain relationships with those who do not care about your financial status.
